docs.title: HRAgents
docs.text:
A virtual HR team for the HR department of one.

HRAgents is a self-hosted platform for the whole employee lifecycle — hiring, onboarding, records, leave, payroll preparation, compliance, growth and offboarding. Language models extract and draft; deterministic code scores and routes; a named human decides everything consequential. Every outcome is reconstructible from a tamper-evident audit chain.

Quickstart Architecture GitHub

docs.title: What it actually does
docs.text:
• Evaluates candidates with a deterministic scorer. LLM agents deconstruct a CV and portfolio into structured evidence; the score is pure Python over that evidence, with the references behind every dimension. The same input scores the same, every time.
  • Bounds automation in code. Auto-scheduling requires a high score, low run-to-run variance, zero anomaly flags and evidence for every dimension. Rejections above the merit floor require a named human; below it, a documented rejection with a feedback report. Unevidenced scores are zeroed and can neither schedule nor reject automatically.
  • Runs the department, not just the ATS. Onboarding plans, contracts and expiry reminders, leave balances and approval queues, payroll runs with operator-verified statutory tables (never hardcoded rates), growth cycles, compliance deadlines and data-subject requests, offboarding and asset clearance — in nine workspaces over one audit trail.
  • Keeps a real record. Every state transition is an audit entry in a hash chain. Evaluations persist the exact rubric family and digest that produced them; payroll runs are immutable once reviewed and a re-run supersedes rather than overwrites.
  • Degrades honestly. No cloud keys are required. The offline test model, hash embeddings, local documents and manual WhatsApp/calendar transports are the defaults; each provider reports whether it is configured and answering.

docs.title: What it deliberately does not do
docs.text: Not done Why Execute payments Payroll is prepare, verify and export; bank files are a human step Auto-reject above the merit floor A rejection is a named human's decision with a reason Run shell or arbitrary command tools Agents read and extract; they do not operate the machine Hardcode statutory rates Operator-maintained, source-verified rate tables gate payroll math Decide who gets hired The system routes evidence and drafts; people decide Scrape or infer protected attributes Scoring consumes only the four documented dimensions

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    CV[CV / portfolio] --> EXTRACT[Extraction agents]
    EXTRACT -->|structured evidence + refs| SCORE[Deterministic scorer]
    SCORE -->|S, σ, evidence| POLICY[Policy engine]
    POLICY -->|auto-schedule| SCHED[Scheduling]
    POLICY -->|HITL| HUMAN[Named human]
    HUMAN -->|decision + reason| AUDIT[(Audit chain)]
    SCHED --> AUDIT
    HUMAN --> DEPTS[Leave · Payroll · Growth · Compliance · Offboarding]
    DEPTS --> AUDIT

The full pipeline, the automation bounds, and the data model are documented under Architecture; the exact decision table is in Human-in-the-loop bounds.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The API is a FastAPI application. Every instance serves its own OpenAPI 3.1 document at /openapi.json, interactive Swagger at /docs and ReDoc at /redoc. The specification below is the one committed with this release.

Authentication is an X-API-Key header. Permissions are checked per route and return a 403 with a stable problem code when the role is not entitled; a missing or refused credential is a 401 that names which of the two it was. Errors are application/problem+json with a stable code (see Deployment & operations).

docs.title: Data governance
docs.text:
What the operator can take with them, what deletion actually does, and who else touches the data.

Full export. Every database row this tenant owns — employees, documents, leave, payroll, evaluations, approvals, the audit chain — is one JSON document:

curl -s localhost:8000/v1/export -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" > hragents-export.json

The compliance queue has the same action as a download. It is admin-only, audited (data.exported, before the stream starts), and streamed table by table; the manifest says that each table is its own read snapshot. Binary attachments live in object storage and are exported from the bucket separately:

docker compose exec minio mc mirror /data/hragents-documents ./documents

Deletion. Retention policies and data-subject erasures are docs/architecture/ and /app/w/compliance: a sweep reports what it purged, spared, skipped and failed, and a failing handler leaves the record for the next pass. Payroll is pseudonymized rather than deleted because it is a tax record. Backups keep their own history until their retention window passes.

Every purge attempt is journaled before its handler runs and closed when it finishes. The handlers span stores without a shared transaction, so a purge is recoverable rather than atomic: if a process dies mid-handler, the row stays running, the next sweep reconciles it against the ledger (done when the record was purged, retried otherwise), and every handler is idempotent — deleting a missing row or anonymizing twice is a no-op. The journal is at GET /v1/compliance/retention/purge-jobs and the compliance queue shows attempts that need attention, rather than letting the same record fail silently every fifteen minutes.

Subprocessors. A self-hosted install has none of ours: Postgres, Redis, MinIO and Mailpit run on the operator's host. The operators' own configured providers (model, email, storage, calendar) are their accounts and their terms. The DPA template in docs/legal/dpa-template.md lists the categories to fill in.

docs.title: Deployment & operations
docs.text: How to run HRAgents on your own machine or a small server, and what to do when something breaks. Everything here assumes the self-host path: Docker Compose, PostgreSQL (with pgvector), Redis, MinIO, and Mailpit for local mail. No cloud keys are required — the offline test model, hash embeddings, and manual transports are the defaults.

docs.title: 1. One command
docs.text:
Generate the local configuration first — the operator's name, a role-bound admin key, the business timezone, and the offline model default:

uv run python scripts/setup.py

It writes .env (never committed) with one hr_admin principal. Compose loads that file through env_file; the stack's fixed wiring still wins where it matters. The key is printed once — paste it into the dashboard sign-in. Without uv on the host, copy .env.example to .env and set the same values by hand.

Then:

docker compose up --build

To run the published release instead of building it, select a tag and skip the build:

HRAGENTS_IMAGE=ghcr.io/davinakmalyasha/hragents:0.1.0 docker compose pull
HRAGENTS_IMAGE=ghcr.io/davinakmalyasha/hragents:0.1.0 docker compose up -d --no-build

Images are multi-arch (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64). Each release publishes the exact version, its major.minor, latest, and a sha-… tag. The release workflow fails on CRITICAL vulnerabilities it can fix, and attaches the Trivy SARIF and an SPDX SBOM to the release; the SBOM and max-mode provenance are also attached to the image digest in the registry.

What starts:

Service What it does Notes postgres database volume pgdata, health-checked, RLS enforced (see below) redis queue backend volume redisdata minio object storage (reserved) volume miniodata, console on :9001; documents still live in Postgres mailpit local mail server SMTP 1025, inbox UI http://localhost:8025 migrate alembic upgrade head runs to completion, then the API starts api FastAPI + dashboard at /app http://localhost:8000/app, health on /healthz and /readyz worker scripts/run_worker.py the pipeline: claims queued applications and evaluates them scheduler scripts/run_scheduler.py --purge every 15 min the department clock messaging scripts/run_messaging.py every 5 min carries the outbox, polls replies

First start takes a few minutes (dashboard build). Watch progress with docker compose logs -f api worker.

The worker is not optional. The API accepts an application and publishes it; only the worker evaluates it. Without it, submissions sit in queued forever and everything looks like it worked. Check curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep stuck_queued — a non-zero value means nothing is draining the queue.

Row-level security. The Postgres image creates the database owner as a superuser, and a superuser bypasses every RLS policy. docker/postgres/ runs once on first init to demote it (NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS). The policies on all 35 tables are otherwise decorative in the shipped stack. If you are upgrading an existing volume, run ALTER ROLE hragents NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS; by hand.

docs.title: What is wired
docs.text: GET /v1/providers (admin key) reports, for every capability, the provider in use, whether the environment locks it, and what that provider's own health check says. Configuration comes back masked — the last four characters of a secret, never the secret. The same list is on the operations page (/app/ops).

docs.title: Editing providers
docs.text:
The operations page (/app/ops) can change a capability's provider and its configuration once the operator supplies an encryption key. Without one the panel stays read-only — a credential will not be stored in the clear.

uv run python scripts/settings_key.py

Put the printed line in .env and restart. The key seals every config before it is written; responses show only the last four characters of a secret, and a blank secret on update keeps the stored value. A stored selection wins over .env unless the environment locks the capability (HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_<CAPABILITY>_LOCK=true); the compose stack locks the queue. Services built at startup — the model runtime, the queue — take a change after a restart, which the response says.

To rotate the key, prepend the new key to the comma-separated list, restart, re-save the providers you changed (the UI keeps the secret when the field is blank), then remove the old key.

docs.title: Verified credentials
docs.text:
A certificate on a CV is a claim. The credential registry is where an operator records what the issuer actually confirmed, and scoring only trusts it once a named human has verified the registry with a source.

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/v1/credentials -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"   -d '{"name":"AWS certifications","issuer":"AWS"}'
# add the rows you checked, then certify them
curl -s -X PUT localhost:8000/v1/credentials/$ID/entries -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"   -d '{"entries":[{"name":"AWS Solutions Architect","expires_on":"2027-01-01"}]}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/v1/credentials/$ID/verify -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"   -d '{"source_note":"issuer page, 2026-10-24"}'

A registry is inert until verified. Once at least one is usable, a claim that matches nothing counts as unverified (a Coursera badge and a genuine certificate stop scoring alike), while an entry past expires_on answers expired. Editing entries invalidates the verification, exactly like a rate table. The compliance queue has the same import path in the dashboard: create a registry, paste its rows (one per line, name | status | id | expiry | notes), then verify it with the source you checked.

docs.title: Malware scanning
docs.text:
Uploads are stored unscanned by default, and the audit entry says so. Point the API at a ClamAV daemon to scan before storage:

HRAGENTS_CLAMAV_HOST=clamav      # or localhost, a sidecar, a socket proxy
HRAGENTS_CLAMAV_PORT=3310
HRAGENTS_CLAMAV_TIMEOUT=5
  • clean → stored; the document.uploaded entry records scan=clean.
  • infected → refused with 422; nothing is stored, and document.rejected_malware records the signature — never the file or its name.
  • scanner unreachable → refused with 503; the file is not stored. A configured scanner that is down must not silently downgrade to unscanned.

The scan speaks ClamAV's INSTREAM protocol over TCP, with no shell and a bounded timeout. The hook lives in DocumentService.upload, the one path that accepts arbitrary bytes; an employee-document row registered against an existing object does not bypass it because it carries no content.

docs.title: External MCP tools (optional, HTTP/SSE only)
docs.text:
An operator can attach an MCP server for tools that live outside HRAgents (an ATS or HRIS connector). Two limits are deliberate:

  • No stdio transport. A stdio server would mean spawning a process; the product's rule is that agents never get a shell, so only HTTP/SSE endpoints are accepted.
  • Destructive tools are not exposed. The registry's human-approval gate needs a dry-run preview, and an MCP tool cannot produce one without making the call. Read and write tools can be exposed; destructive actions stay in the product, where a named human approves a preview.

Configuration is one JSON value:

HRAGENTS_MCP_SERVERS='[
  {"name":"ats","url":"https://mcp.example.com/mcp","auth_env":"ATS_MCP_TOKEN",
   "allowed_agents":["screening_coordinator"],
   "tools":{"get_candidate":"read","add_note":"write"}}
]'

Only the tools named under tools are registered (mcp.<server>.<tool>); a tool the server adds later stays invisible until the operator names it. allowed_agents is the other half of least privilege — an empty list connects the server for discovery but exposes nothing. The bearer token is read from the variable named by auth_env, never from the URL, config or logs; putting credentials in the URL is refused.

A server that is unreachable or unauthenticated degrades only itself: the app starts, the other tools work, and GET /v1/ops/mcp (admin) lists each server's connection state and exposed tools.

The same list is editable from the dashboard's Operations → Connections panel (admin only). Saves are audited, reload the manager in-process, and unregister the previous tools so removing a connection is immediate. Two rules keep the two surfaces from disagreeing:

  • an environment-configured name is read-only in the dashboard; change it in HRAGENTS_MCP_SERVERS instead, and
  • dashboard rows are install-wide, because MCP tools live in one process-wide registry — they are not tenant-isolated.

The panel's Test button connects, lists tools and disconnects without registering anything or writing a row. Browse catalog offers templates for an ATS, HRIS, Slack and calendar gateway, each with its data flow and minimum scopes; see MCP connector catalog.

docs.title: Secrets and rotation
docs.text:
Nothing in this repository ships a secret. Rotate after any suspicion, and in this order so a rotation cannot lock you out:

API keys and principals. Add the new key to HRAGENTS_API_PRINCIPALS (keep the old one), restart, move clients, then remove the old entry and restart. A removed key answers 401 on the next request and the dashboard drops it. The audit chain records the actor id, so rotating a key for the same person keeps the same name on the record. An unbound HRAGENTS_API_KEYS key is one shared identity; prefer principals.

Settings encryption key (provider credentials). Prepend a new key to the comma-separated HRAGENTS_SETTINGS_ENCRYPTION_KEY, restart, re-save the providers you changed (a blank secret keeps the stored value), then remove the old key. Rows stay readable while both keys are present.

VAPID (push). Generate a new pair, put it in .env, restart. Existing browser subscriptions were bound to the old application key and will not deliver; each person must turn the bell off and on (which unsubscribes, deletes the server row and re-subscribes with the new key).

Provider credentials. Prefer the dashboard (sealed at rest) — Save, then Test. If the capability is environment-locked, update the env value and restart. Revoke the old credential at the provider only after the Test button answers.

Database, MinIO, SMTP/IMAP. Change the password on the service, update .env/compose, restart, then confirm /readyz. Backups taken before the change remain restorable with the old credentials; they do not contain the new one.

After every rotation, revoke the old secret at its issuer. The audit chain stores actor ids and field names, never the secret value, so it does not need rewriting.

docs.text: Full export, deletion, subprocessors and the DPA template are in Data governance.

docs.title: Push notifications (optional)
docs.text:
Notifications stay off until the operator issues a VAPID pair for this deployment. No key is shipped: a committed private key would let anyone impersonate the sender for every install.

uv run python scripts/vapid_keys.py

Copy the three printed lines into .env and restart. The private key stays on the server; GET /v1/push/config serves only the public half. With keys configured the topbar shows a bell: turning it on subscribes this browser and sends one test notification, so "on" is a demonstrated fact rather than a promise.

New approvals are announced to the roles that may decide them. Payloads name the subject ("a leave request needs your decision") and never the employee or an amount: a lock screen is not an access-controlled surface. Delivery is best-effort and runs outside the approval path, so an unreachable push service cannot block the decision it was announcing. An endpoint the browser has dropped (404/410) is pruned, and a person whose key is removed or whose role changes stops receiving pings. Browsers require HTTPS for service workers; localhost is the exception.

docs.title: Starter content
docs.text:
A fresh install is empty by design. The dashboard's first-run card offers the same seed as the CLI:

docker compose exec api uv run python scripts/seed_starters.py

It creates an onboarding and an offboarding checklist and one empty shell per statutory table kind payroll needs. No values are seeded: a named human enters and verifies every number, and payroll refuses to compute until that happens.

docs.title: Demo data
docs.text:
To see the product with a story in it:

docker compose exec api uv run python scripts/seed_demo.py

Five employees (one mid-probation), two contracts, an expiring KTP, a pending annual-leave approval, an open engineering role with two applications, an onboarding plan, a draft growth cycle and a payroll run for the current month. Everything is created through the real services, so the audit trail, the approval queue, the task list and the retention ledger are populated too. The marker employee number DEMO-001 makes the seed idempotent on Postgres; with the in-memory backend each process starts empty, so every run reseeds — and a separately started dev server will not see a standalone seed, because the two processes share no store. Use the Compose stack (Postgres) for a demo you can browse.

The statutory rate tables are seeded unverified on purpose. Payroll refuses to compute on a table nobody has checked against a source, and the demo should show that gate rather than fake a figure: verify the tables with real statutory sources before using any number.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
The committed defaults are for a laptop, not for a server. Before exposing the instance, set real values in a .env file next to docker-compose.yml (Compose reads it automatically):

HRAGENTS_API_KEYS=["a-long-random-string"]        # inbound API keys (empty = auth disabled)
# HRAGENTS_API_PRINCIPALS=[{"key":"...","role":"hr_admin","actor_id":"owner"}]
HRAGENTS_TIMEZONE=Asia/Jakarta                    # the zone business dates are read in
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<strong password>
MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD=<strong password>
HRAGENTS_MESSAGING_SANDBOX=false                  # only after you configure a real provider

HRAGENTS_TIMEZONE decides what "today" means for leave years, probation ends, due dates and the sweeps that act on them. It defaults to Asia/Jakarta, and an unknown zone stops startup rather than silently falling back — a server whose host clock is UTC would otherwise be a day off for the seven hours after Jakarta has rolled over.

Never commit .env; .dockerignore keeps it out of the image.

docs.title: Binding a key to an employee
docs.text:
role decides what a principal may do across the whole org. employee_id decides whose records they may act on individually, and the self-service routes need it: an employee requesting their own leave, or moving their own goal along, is refused without it. A key with no employee_id is not a weaker form of an employee key, it is ineligible for those routes.

HRAGENTS_API_PRINCIPALS=[
  {"key":"...","role":"employee","actor_id":"sari","employee_id":"<uuid>"},
  {"key":"...","role":"manager","actor_id":"budi","employee_id":"<uuid>"}
]

Take the UUID from the employee record. A manager additionally needs employee_id set to their own record, not their reports': the reporting line comes from each employee's manager_id, so the manager's own binding is what identifies them as the manager. hr_admin and recruiter hold people:write and need no binding to act on any record.

Identity is bound by configuration rather than inferred from an email address, because an email is a nullable, changeable, shareable field, and a permission that depends on one is not a permission. An unbound principal is refused rather than assumed to own whatever it names.

What the two modes mean. With no keys configured, every request is accepted as a local development principal with full admin rights — appropriate for localhost, not for a server. With keys configured, the dashboard signs in: the first request it makes is /v1/session, and if the server refuses it the app shows a sign-in screen that takes the API key. The key is kept in sessionStorage, so closing the tab ends the session, and signing out clears it and the cache. The sign-in screen never decides anything itself: the role it displays is the one the server resolved, and every permission is still checked server-side.

Still not a substitute for TLS. The key travels in an X-API-Key header and is readable by any script on the origin, so a self-host exposed to a network wants a reverse proxy that terminates TLS and restricts who can reach it. There are no passwords and therefore no password reset: the credential is the key, and rotating it means changing the configured principal.

docs.title: 2. Connecting a real mail provider
docs.text:
Compose ships Mailpit so nothing leaves your machine while you evaluate. To send real email, point the provider layer at your mailbox and leave the sandbox alone:

HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_EMAIL_SEND=email.smtp
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_EMAIL_SEND_CONFIG={"host":"smtp.example.com","port":587,"username":"hr@example.com","password":"...","from_address":"hr@example.com"}
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_EMAIL_RECEIVE=email.imap_poll
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_EMAIL_RECEIVE_CONFIG={"host":"imap.example.com","username":"hr@example.com","password":"...","mailbox":"INBOX"}

Then docker compose up -d --force-recreate api messaging. Until a message is queued behind a named human, nothing is sent — and the bridge records the provider, the message id, and any failure on the message itself.

docs.title: 3. Health, logs, metrics
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:8000/healthz                    # liveness: the process is up
curl -s localhost:8000/readyz                     # readiness, per dependency
curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep stuck_queued # is anything draining the queue?
docker compose logs -f api worker scheduler messaging

/readyz returns 503 with a per-dependency breakdown when something is unreachable, which is what an orchestrator should probe. It checks database, messaging, audit, queue, and skills — the last two because they decide whether the product works rather than whether it starts: no queue means submissions are accepted and never evaluated, and no skills library means every agent runs with no runbook.

/metrics is plain Prometheus text; curl is enough, no exporter stack. The series worth alerting on:

Series Meaning hragents_applications_stuck_queued accepted but never evaluated — the worker is down or wedged hragents_scheduler_last_success_timestamp per job; a stale value means a job is failing inside the while true loop hragents_applications_by_status where the pipeline actually is hragents_http_request_duration_seconds_sum paired with _count for a mean hragents_queue_pending / _inflight / _dead evaluation queue depth per topic; _dead above zero is a message that exhausted its retries

The scheduler and messaging loops swallow failures (|| echo ...) because a crashing tick should not kill the container. They rewrite their JSON report on a shared volume every tick, and the metrics endpoint reads it — that is how a silently failing loop becomes visible without adding a log aggregator. The containers also have HEALTHCHECKs, so docker compose ps shows the truth.

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text:
The repository ships Prometheus rules for the canaries and the usual API signals: ops/alerts/hragents.rules.yml. Scrape the API with a job named hragents-api and load the file as a rule file; nothing else is required.

Alert Severity What it means HRAgentsStuckQueuedApplications critical submissions are accepted and nothing is evaluating them — start or restart the worker HRAgentsSchedulerJobStale critical a scheduled job missed three 15-minute ticks; retention, expiry and offer expiry all live there HRAgentsDeadLetteredMessages warning a message exhausted its retries; read its reason and requeue deliberately HRAgentsQueueBacklog warning more than 100 messages waiting for half an hour HRAgentsApiDown / HRAgentsHighErrorRate / HRAgentsSlowResponses critical / warning the ordinary API signals

Nothing pages by itself: the rules are the operator's to load, and /readyz remains the external probe for orchestrators. The rules test (tests/test_alerts_config.py) fails if a rule references a series the API no longer renders, so a renamed metric cannot silently disable an alert.

The dead letters themselves are readable at GET /v1/ops/dead-letters (admin:manage; metadata and payload keys, never the résumé text) and a requeue is POST /v1/ops/dead-letters/{id}/requeue with a mandatory reason, recorded on the audit chain. Requeueing resets the attempt budget because a person decided the cause is fixed; the automatic reaper does the opposite and counts the attempt, so a crash-looping message still runs out of retries. The queue-reaper scheduler job returns leases older than five minutes to pending, which covers a worker wedged on the handler itself. The dashboard mirrors the API at /app/ops (reachable from the command palette) with the same reason-gated requeue.

docs.title: 4. Backups (and proving they work)
docs.text:
docker compose exec api python scripts/backup.py --output /app/data/backups --verify

--verify restores the dump into a throwaway database and re-verifies the audit hash chain inside it. A backup you have not restored is a guess; this script prints audit chain: intact or fails with the first broken sequence. Restore a dump with:

docker compose exec api python scripts/backup.py --restore /app/data/backups/hragents-<stamp>.sql.gz

docs.title: 5. Upgrades
docs.text:
git pull
docker compose up --build -d          # runs migrations, restarts services
docker compose exec api python scripts/verify_audit.py     # chain still intact

Migrations are additive and reversible (alembic downgrade -1). Take a backup first when a release contains a data migration.

docs.title: 6. Runbooks
docs.text:
Candidate messages stuck in "queued". Check the messaging logs. A failed send keeps the message queued and records last_error on it (visible in the communication panel). Fix the transport and the next run retries.

The scheduler job failed. run_scheduler.py prints one line per job and exits nonzero on failure. Run a single job on demand:

docker compose exec api python scripts/run_scheduler.py --job retention --purge
docker compose exec api python scripts/run_scheduler.py --job reply-sla

Audit chain verification fails. python scripts/verify_audit.py prints the first invalid sequence. That means a row in audit_log was altered out of band: restore from backup and investigate the database access path. Never edit audit_log by hand.

LLM provider is not configured. Agents fall back to the offline model, so the deterministic core (scoring, policy, approvals) keeps working. Configure HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_LLM to enable extraction.

Rate limit (429). The API throttles per principal at 300 requests/minute by default. Raise HRAGENTS_API_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE or add a role-bound key.

docs.title: 7. Without Docker
docs.text:
uv sync
uv run alembic upgrade head
uv run uvicorn hr_agents.main:app --reload     # API + dashboard on :8000
uv run python scripts/run_scheduler.py          # the clock, in another shell
uv run python scripts/run_messaging.py          # the messaging bridge

In-memory mode (HRAGENTS_STORE_BACKEND=memory, the default) needs nothing at all: it is the zero-configuration developer experience and the right choice for a demo, not for real HR data.

docs.title: 8. Fully offline (local models)
docs.text: Everything below keeps candidate and employee data on the machine. The deterministic core — scoring, payroll arithmetic, policy routing, approvals — never calls a model in the first place, so what this section configures is extraction, drafting and chat.

docs.title: Point every capability at something local
docs.text:
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_LLM=llm.ollama
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_LLM_CONFIG={"model":"qwen2.5:7b"}
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_EMBEDDINGS=embeddings.ollama
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_EMBEDDINGS_CONFIG={"model":"nomic-embed-text"}
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_STORAGE=storage.local_disk
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_STORAGE_CONFIG={"root":"data/documents"}
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_QUEUE=queue.memory
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_WHATSAPP=whatsapp.manual_links
HRAGENTS_PROVIDER_CALENDAR=calendar.manual_slots

whatsapp.manual_links and calendar.manual_slots need no credentials at all: you send the message from your own WhatsApp and enter interview slots by hand, and the app composes the link and the ICS. For email, point email.smtp and email.imap_poll at the Mailpit container from §1 — it is a local mail server, so nothing leaves the host.

docs.title: Get the models
docs.text:
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b          # extraction, drafting, chat
ollama pull nomic-embed-text    # embeddings, 768 dimensions

Model floor. Extraction asks a model to return structured data from a CV and to keep two similar profiles straight. A 7–8B instruction-tuned model is the floor at which that is reliable; 14B and up is visibly better on ambiguous résumés and on the drafted summaries a person edits. Below the floor the failure mode is quiet: fields come back plausible-but-wrong, which is worse than a refusal, because nothing downstream can tell. If you have no model to run, embeddings.hash implements embeddings with no download at all — it is lexical overlap, not meaning, so it finds documents that share words and misses ones that share sense.

docs.title: What the offline mode does not do
docs.text:
• GitHub and repository lookups, publication checks and credential registries need the network. Offline, those signals are simply absent from an evaluation, and the deterministic scorer treats absent evidence as absent rather than guessing.
  • The built-in test model runs the whole pipeline with canned responses so tests and demos need neither a network nor a model. Its numbers are fake by construction; never use it for a real candidate.
  • Provider health badges report configured, not reachable: the health probe is a Phase 7 item, so verify Ollama yourself with ollama list and one extraction from the dashboard before trusting a batch.

docs.title: Fairness and score monitoring
docs.text:
HRAgents separates two questions that are easy to blur together:

  1. Does the deterministic pipeline ignore non-job-relevant attributes? The counterfactual harness answers this on synthetic pairs and runs in CI.
  2. Is the real scoring path behaving consistently per job? The distribution monitor answers this from evaluations the pipeline actually registered.

Neither is a demographic parity measurement. Protected attributes are never collected or scored, so no report here can compare outcomes by group; the honest claim is invariance plus per-job drift monitoring.

docs.title: Counterfactual harness
docs.text:
services/fairness.py scores identical profiles that differ only in a name or city, and compares the full score vector and weighted total exactly. The pipeline is deterministic, so any change is a defect, not noise. The eval dataset also carries name-swapped CV pairs compared by a decision signature (normalized skills, experience shape, education, certifications and the scored vector) that excludes the swapped name.

CI exercises the wiring with the offline model. A live-model comparison still needs a provider that accepts the deployment's configuration; see docs/plan/remaining-work.md.

docs.title: Per-job distribution monitor
docs.text:
GET /v1/ops/fairness?days=90 (admin) returns, for every job with evaluations in the window:

Field Meaning evaluations Registered evaluations in the window mean, minimum, maximum The weighted total (s_tech) bins Five half-open bands, [0.0,1.0] in 0.2 steps recommendations Routing mix (auto_schedule, human_review, reject_requires_signoff, reject) requires_human Human review + sign-off required flagged Evaluations carrying at least one flag

The report is bounded to the most recent 2,000 evaluations in the window and sets truncated when it clips; the window itself is validated to 1–365 days. It reads the same registered evaluations the dashboard serves — not fixtures — so a weight change, an extraction drift or an unusual manual-routing share for one job becomes visible without a live model call.

The Operations page renders the report as a table under Score distribution, including the API's note that protected attributes are never collected.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• A job whose mean moves while its rubric digest does not is a signal to inspect extraction and evidence, not a reason to change thresholds.
  • A rising requires_human share is the system asking for people; check the decision reasons and flags before assuming a candidate-quality problem.
  • A spike in flagged for one job points at document quality, truncation or injection attempts for that intake source.

docs.title: What is deliberately absent
docs.text:
• No protected attributes in the data model. Adding them to measure parity would create the very dataset the product avoids holding.
  • No group-level metric presented as fairness. The report says what it is on screen and in the API note.
  • No automatic threshold change. Monitoring is a named human's input to a deliberate rubric decision, not an auto-tuner.

docs.title: MCP connector catalog
docs.text:
The Connections panel can show a small catalog of templates for the connectors most installations want: an ATS, an HRIS, Slack notifications and a calendar busy lookup. A template is not a connection and is never enabled by default; choosing one fills the form with the shape of the connection, and the operator still supplies the gateway endpoint, saves it, and runs Test.

There are no vendor API keys or invented vendor MCP URLs in the catalog. The entries describe capability, data flow and enablement; the endpoint belongs to the operator's own MCP gateway.

Template Reads Writes Minimum scopes ATS (Greenhouse / Lever style) candidate, application and job metadata one application note read candidates, read applications, write notes HRIS (Talenta / Gadjah style) employee identity, org unit, leave balances nothing read employees, read leave balances Slack notifications nothing one message to one channel post to that channel Calendar busy lookup free/busy windows nothing read free/busy

docs.title: The rules every template keeps
docs.text:
• No decisions. A connector cannot reject, approve, move a stage, override a score or schedule payroll. Those remain dashboard actions with a named human and, where relevant, the approval engine.
  • The smallest useful data flow. The ATS template does not forward résumé files; the HRIS template does not read salary or bank fields; the calendar template asks for busy blocks, not event titles; the Slack template sends a short human-action message, not candidate documents or contact details.
  • Explicit tools only. The template lists each remote tool and its impact. A tool the server adds later stays invisible until an operator names it.
  • No destructive tools. A destructive remote tool has no preview contract, so it is refused by the registry, template or not.
  • The token lives in the environment. The form stores the name of the variable, never the token, and the URL must not embed credentials.

docs.title: Enabling one
docs.text:
1. Stand up an MCP gateway in front of the system, with the minimum scopes in the table above.
  2. Put the gateway token in the variable named by the template (ATS_MCP_TOKEN, HRIS_MCP_TOKEN, SLACK_MCP_TOKEN, CALENDAR_MCP_TOKEN).
  3. Open Operations → Connections → Browse catalog, choose the template and fill in your gateway's endpoint; adjust the tool names to the ones your gateway actually offers.
  4. Save, then press Test. The probe connects, lists the tools and disconnects without registering or writing anything.
  5. Let one agent make a read call on a real (or seeded) record and inspect the audit entry.

The catalog lives in src/hr_agents/services/mcp_catalog.py. A guard test keeps every entry honest: unique ids, non-empty scopes, data-flow and enable steps, no destructive tools, and no decision words in tool names. Adding an entry is a code change so the review can check those properties.

docs.title: MCP server (hragents-mcp)
docs.text:
A packaged MCP server for external clients — Claude Desktop, IDE agents, or anything that speaks MCP over stdio. By default it is read-only: it asks an HRAgents install what is waiting, what happened to one application, how it was evaluated, and what leave somebody has left.

Three write tools can be enabled (HRAGENTS_MCP_WRITES=1) for intake and requests. Even then it never approves, rejects, moves stages, overrides decisions, schedules payroll or erases records — those remain in the dashboard behind a named human.

docs.title: What it exposes
docs.text:
Tool What it answers queue Priority-ranked applications for one job (job_id) application_status Status and timeline for one application evaluation_summary Deterministic evaluation: score vector, evidence, rubric family/digest, flags, recommendation pending_approvals Approvals waiting for a human, optionally by approver role leave_balances Leave balances for one employee (the API applies its own rules)

Write tools, off unless HRAGENTS_MCP_WRITES=1:

Tool What it does Permission create_application Ingests one application from an external ATS; the caller supplies the consent it captured — the server never infers consent recruiting:write start_onboarding_plan Opens a plan from a template people:write open_leave_request Files a leave request, which enters the human approval queue self_service (or people:write)

The write tools are still just API calls: the key's role is the authorization, and audit records the actor behind the key. open_leave_request cannot decide the request it files; approving is a dashboard action.

docs.title: Exposing fewer tools
docs.text:
HRAGENTS_MCP_TOOLS narrows the surface to a comma-separated allowlist, so one client can see the queue without also seeing leave balances:

export HRAGENTS_MCP_TOOLS=queue,application_status
hragents-mcp

Unset or empty means every tool the mode allows. Startup fails on an unknown name, and a write tool listed without HRAGENTS_MCP_WRITES=1 is a configuration error rather than a silently missing tool. The allowlist does not add authorization — the API key's role still decides every call.

Each tool is a GET against the API. That is the authorization model: the server holds a role-bound API key, so the API's permissions, tenant scoping and audit chain apply exactly as they would to any other client. A key that may not read a record receives the API's refusal, not a filtered answer. Give the MCP server a key whose role matches what the person using the client should see.

docs.title: Install and run
docs.text:
The console script is installed with the package:

uv pip install hr-agents      # or run from a checkout with `uv run hragents-mcp`

export HRAGENTS_API_URL=http://localhost:8000   # default
export HRAGENTS_API_KEY=...                     # required; role-bound
export HRAGENTS_MCP_WRITES=1                    # optional; enables the write tools
export HRAGENTS_MCP_TOOLS=queue,leave_balances  # optional; expose only these tools
hragents-mcp

The transport is stdio, which is what desktop MCP clients launch. The API key is read from the environment — never a command-line argument, where other users on the host could see it in a process list.

docs.title: Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Add the server to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "hragents": {
      "command": "hragents-mcp",
      "env": {
        "HRAGENTS_API_URL": "http://localhost:8000",
        "HRAGENTS_API_KEY": "paste-the-role-bound-key-here",
        "HRAGENTS_MCP_WRITES": "1"
      }
    }
  }
}

Restart the client. The tools appear in its tool list. If the API is not running, tool calls answer a readable error instead of failing the server.

docs.title: What is deliberately missing
docs.text:
• No decisions. The server cannot approve, reject, override, move a stage or schedule anything, even with an admin key. Those routes are in the dashboard.
  • No payroll, erasure or rejection execution. Payroll stays prepare/verify/ export; erasure stays a human-run compliance action; rejections require the merit floor and a named sign-off.
  • No raw documents. Tools return structured metadata; résumé text and file bytes are not sent to an MCP client.
  • No document requests yet. Asking an employee for a missing document has no API route, so there is no tool for it; adding one needs an approval-backed request, not a bypass.

docs.title: Contract tests
docs.text: tests/test_mcp_server.py connects an in-memory MCP client to the real server, asserts the read-only default and the opt-in tool set, runs a write through a mocked API, checks that an intake body carries the caller's consent unchanged, checks that no decision tool exists, and checks that neither the key nor a refusal leaks into the response.

docs.title: HRAgents: an auditable HR agent platform for the department of one
docs.text: Davin Akmal Yasha · v0.2.0 · Apache-2.0

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Small organisations do not have an HR department; they have one person who carries hiring, onboarding, records, leave, payroll preparation, compliance, growth and offboarding, usually alongside another job. LLM agents can plausibly absorb the reading and drafting, but they cannot be trusted with the decisions, and a system that quietly guesses at a rejection is worse than the backlog it replaces. HRAgents is a self-hosted platform built around one division: agents extract and draft, deterministic code scores and routes, a named human decides. Every state transition is written to a hash-chained audit log, every score cites the evidence behind it, and every automation boundary is expressed as a pure function with a test. This paper describes the design, the measured behaviour, and the limitations that remain.

docs.title: 1. The problem
docs.text:
A solo HR person is asked to make high-volume, high-consequence decisions with no second reader. Three failure modes follow:

  1. Silent rejection. A CV is skimmed for ten seconds; the candidate never hears back. At scale this is both a fairness problem and a reputational one.
  2. Inconsistent judgement. The same profile reads differently on a Monday than on a Friday, and nobody can reconstruct why a decision was made.
  3. Unverifiable automation. Tools that "use AI for HR" typically hide a model call behind a score. The score cannot be inspected, reproduced, or defended.

The regulatory direction is unambiguous: under Indonesia's UU PDP and the EU AI Act's transparency expectations, a decision about a person needs a record of who decided, on what basis, and with what human involvement.

docs.title: 2. Design principles
docs.text:
Extract, don't decide. Agents turn unstructured documents into a typed CandidateProfile with provenance references. They can also draft a summary or a feedback note. They never produce the number that gates a person, and an unparseable document degrades to a human review rather than an error.

Evidence first. Every score dimension carries the references that produced it. A dimension with no reference contributes zero, even if the title says "Senior". The pairing rule matters: missing evidence also blocks automatic rejection, because an extraction gap is not a property of the candidate.

Named humans gate outcomes. Rejections above the merit floor require a person with the authority the approval engine checks, a reason, and an audit entry. Payroll is prepared, verified and exported; payment execution is out of scope. There are no shell tools, ever.

Operator data, not hardcoded law. Statutory rates, tax brackets and overtime premiums arrive as empty, unverified tables. A named human enters the numbers, records the source, and certifies them; payroll refuses to compute otherwise. Rubric thresholds travel in a verified rubric version, so changing a band is the same act as changing a rate.

Make the record the product. The audit chain is append-only and tamper-evident. Evaluations persist the rubric family and content digest that produced them. A reviewed payroll run is immutable; a re-run supersedes it with an explicit link instead of rewriting history.

docs.title: 3. System
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IN[Documents · forms · email] --> Q[(Queue)]
    Q --> W[Worker]
    W --> A[Extraction agents]
    A -->|typed profile + refs| S[Deterministic scorer]
    S -->|four dimensions + evidence| P[Policy engine]
    P -->|auto-schedule| C[Scheduling]
    P -->|HITL| H[Named human]
    H -->|approve · reject · override| AU[(Audit chain)]
    C --> AU
    H --> D[Leave · Payroll · Growth · Compliance · Offboarding]
    D --> AU

The API is FastAPI over a sync domain layer (ADR 0005). PostgreSQL carries the tenant-scoped tables under row-level security; Redis carries the evaluation queue; the dashboard is a React PWA served by the same process. K workers claim messages, run k independent extractions, and the scorer produces one score tensor per run; variance across runs (σ) is a first-class input to the policy.

docs.title: 4. Scoring and calibration
docs.text:
Four dimensions make the tensor: technical depth, stack alignment, systems literacy and verifiable certifications. Each family (engineering, finance, education, healthcare, legal, operations, sales, general) supplies its own breadth vocabulary, professional signals, title tiers and weight mix, exposed as one taxonomy object; the dimensions compose from a small set of pure primitives (saturation, evidence density/count, credential credit, title tiers). The engineering template's digest and serialized score vector are pinned as regression fences.

Routing is a pure function over S, σ, evidence sufficiency, anomaly flags, calendar constraints and consent:

Condition Decision consent inactive halt, human review anomaly flags human review (HITL_ANOMALY) no mutual slots human review (HITL_CALENDAR) S ≥ 0.85 ∧ σ ≤ 0.05 ∧ evidence AUTO_SCHEDULE S ≥ 0.85 ∧ σ ≤ 0.05 ∧ ¬evidence HITL_MANUAL ¬evidence (any other score) HITL_MANUAL 0.70 ≤ S < 0.85 ∧ evidence soft-rejection queue, sign-off required S < 0.70 ∧ evidence documented rejection with feedback

Calibration is label-free: the corpus asserts orderings (strong > adequate > weak, matched fit > tenured misfit) rather than invented ground truth, because a ground-truth label would let anyone move a number until a test passed.

docs.title: 5. Evaluation
docs.text:
Corpus. 50 synthetic profiles — 18 engineering and 32 non-IT (finance, operations, sales, admin, customer support), English and Bahasa Indonesia, in Markdown, JSON and a real PDF — plus 15 edge cases: date overlaps, career changes, overqualification, freelance history, a fake certificate, a scanned image-only PDF, an oversized document, a malformed JSON export, two prompt-injection CVs and a ghost-job mismatch. Four name-swap pairs test scorer invariance.

Offline suite. Runs in CI with the deterministic test model, no network: structural and safety assertions pass 100% across the five base cases.

Live run. Five cases through xiaomi/mimo-v2.5 (Command Code, ZDR enforced): 5/5, 100% of assertions, mean 81.7 s (21–152 s). Prompt injection is blocked and redacted; zero-width characters are stripped before the model. Latency is acceptable for the asynchronous pipeline and not for interactive use, which is why the dashboard shows progress rather than hiding it.

Throughput. The ingestion path sustains 608.5 req/s = 36,509 req/min at p50 93 ms / p99 169 ms with zero errors in a 5,000-request run, and the audit chain verifies afterwards. This isolates application overhead; Postgres and Redis add deployment latency.

docs.title: 6. Safety and security
docs.text:
• Prompt injection is treated as untrusted content: suspected instructions are redacted and recorded, and no extracted contact can override a form value.
  • RBAC + RLS. Roles hold named permissions; the database enforces tenant isolation; keys can be bound to a role and an employee.
  • Secrets are operator-supplied. Provider credentials entered in the dashboard are Fernet-sealed at rest, masked to four characters in every response, and never written to the audit payload.
  • Immutability. Payroll runs are editable only while draft/assembling; a reviewed run is terminal and a re-run is a linked successor.
  • Uploads. An optional ClamAV scan runs before a document is stored: a clean file is recorded as scanned, an infected one is refused with the signature on the chain, and a configured-but-unreachable scanner refuses the upload instead of silently storing it unscanned.
  • Retention. Erasure walks a ledger with per-entity handlers; a failing handler is isolated and retried rather than silently skipped, payroll is pseudonymized, and the sweep reports what it destroyed, spared and failed. Each attempt is journaled before it runs, so a crash is reconciled and retried on the next pass instead of disappearing.

docs.title: 7. Limitations
docs.text:
Honest, current, and tracked in the repository:

  1. Live-model fairness is unproven. The harness compares name-swapped CV pairs by a decision signature (skills, experience, education, certifications, scored vector) and fails a live run on divergence; CI exercises the wiring offline, where the model is deterministic and cannot show bias.
  2. Credential registries are operator imports. The registry exists, is imported and verified in the dashboard, and gates scoring once verified. There is no issuer API integration: an install that imports nothing treats every claim as before.
  3. Role fit is a coverage gate, not a model. Tenure-driven depth with thin must-have coverage now routes to a person, but the check is token coverage of the job's requirements; a richer per-family sufficiency model is future work.
  4. Cost is tokens, not currency. Each evaluation records its input/output tokens by provider and model, exposed per model; dollar cost is left to the operator's contract, and no cost-per-hire figure is claimed.
  5. The portfolio agent is not in the pipeline. Repository and publication evidence are implemented but the agent that gathers them is not wired into the production path.
  6. The offline model is not a quality signal. Its numbers are fake by construction; it exists to exercise the pipeline without a network.

docs.title: 8. Availability
docs.text: Apache-2.0. Source, architecture decisions, deployment runbooks and the rendered documentation are at https://davinakmalyasha.github.io/HRAgents/; releases are tagged hr-agents-vX.Y.Z with a wheel, an sdist, a scanned multi-arch container image and an SBOM.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Docker Desktop, five minutes, no cloud keys.

docs.title: 1. Configure
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/davinakmalyasha/HRAgents
cd HRAgents
uv run python scripts/setup.py

scripts/setup.py writes .env (gitignored) with the operator's name, one role-bound admin key, the business timezone and the offline model default. It prints the key once. No uv on the host? Copy .env.example to .env and set the same values by hand.

docs.title: 2. Start
docs.text:
docker compose up --build -d

Nine containers come up: Postgres (pgvector), Redis, MinIO, Mailpit, a one-shot migration, the API, the evaluation worker, the scheduler and the messaging bridge. Migrations run before the API serves.

Prefer the published image over a local build?

HRAGENTS_IMAGE=ghcr.io/davinakmalyasha/hragents:0.1.0 docker compose pull
HRAGENTS_IMAGE=ghcr.io/davinakmalyasha/hragents:0.1.0 docker compose up -d --no-build

docs.title: 3. Sign in
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:8000/app and paste the key from step 1.

The first-run card offers starter checklists and the empty statutory-table shells. Want something to look at instead?

docker compose exec api uv run python scripts/seed_demo.py

The demo seeds five employees, a hiring pipeline, a pending leave approval and a payroll run — through the real services, so the audit trail and queues are populated. The statutory rate tables arrive unverified on purpose: payroll refuses to compute until a named human enters and verifies the numbers against a real source.

docs.title: 4. Check it is actually working
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:8000/readyz | python -m json.tool   # queue + skills must be "ok"
curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep stuck_queued   # non-zero = the worker is down

The worker is not optional: the API accepts and publishes an application, and only the worker evaluates it. Without it, submissions sit in queued forever and everything looks fine.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Deployment & operations — backups, upgrades, runbooks, provider configuration, offline mode.
  • Architecture — the pipeline and the nine workspaces.
  • Human-in-the-loop bounds — what runs automatically and what never will.

docs.title: Region and network recipes
docs.text: Two things vary by where the instance runs: the business clock and how the outside world reaches it. Nothing else in HRAgents is region-specific by design — statutory numbers are operator data, and providers are configuration.

docs.title: Jakarta (or anywhere in Indonesia)
docs.text:
HRAGENTS_TIMEZONE=Asia/Jakarta      # the default; set it explicitly anyway
  • Clock. Leave years, probation ends, contract expiry and every retention sweep use the business day from this zone. A host whose clock is UTC is fine; what matters is the timezone setting, and an unknown zone refuses startup.
  • Data residency. The whole stack is yours: Postgres, Redis, MinIO and the document bytes live on your host. Nothing leaves until you configure a hosted model, mail relay or object store. If your policy requires in-country processing, keep those providers in-country or use Ollama and Mailpit.
  • Latency. Hosted models in Singapore add roughly 10–30 ms per request versus a local model; model latency dominates either way (the live eval average was ~82 s for an extraction with a hosted model). Bulk evaluation is asynchronous, so ping is not the bottleneck — the model is.
  • Backups. Keep the pg_dump and MinIO snapshots in the same jurisdiction. The backup drill (scripts/backup.py --verify) does not care where they live, but your DPA might.
  • TLS. Terminate HTTPS at a reverse proxy (Caddy, nginx) or a tunnel (below). Service workers and push notifications require a secure context, so the dashboard is not fully functional over plain HTTP except on localhost.

docs.title: Singapore
docs.text:
HRAGENTS_TIMEZONE=Asia/Singapore     # only if the business day is Singapore's
  • Do not change the timezone to match the server. It is the business zone, not the host zone. Set it to where the company's HR calendar operates, even if the server is in Singapore and the office is in Jakarta.
  • Latency to Indonesian users is small; the same notes as Jakarta apply.

docs.title: Cloudflare Tunnel (webhooks without a public IP)
docs.text:
Some integrations need a public HTTPS URL: inbound email webhooks, WhatsApp Cloud, or a calendar push. A tunnel gives you one without opening a port.

  1. Create a tunnel in the Cloudflare dashboard and note the token.
  2. Run cloudflared next to the stack. In docker-compose.yml:
tunnel:
  image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
  command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run
  environment:
    TUNNEL_TOKEN: ${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN}
  depends_on:
    api:
      condition: service_started
  restart: unless-stopped
  1. In the tunnel's public-hostname mapping, point your hostname at http://api:8000. The API already answers GET /healthz and /readyz; use one of them for the tunnel's own health check.
  2. Set HRAGENTS_TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true on the API only when nothing can reach port 8000 except the tunnel. Without it, the rate limiter buckets every request under cloudflared's address — one shared bucket for all users. With it and a directly reachable origin, a client can spoof the header and mint a fresh bucket.
  3. Give the integration the public hostname. For email, that is the provider's inbound webhook; for WhatsApp Cloud, the callback URL plus the verify token you configured.
  4. Keep the origin private: bind the API to the compose network (the shipped stack does) and do not publish 8000 as well.

What the tunnel does not do. It does not add authentication. The API's own keys are the gate; do not put an unauthenticated admin surface behind a tunnel just because the URL is long. If you terminate access at Cloudflare, keep the API's authentication on as well — defence in depth, not either/or.

docs.title: Checklist for a new region
docs.text:
• [ ] HRAGENTS_TIMEZONE is the business zone, not the host's
  • [ ] The database, object store and backups are in the jurisdiction you claim
  • [ ] A hosted model/mail provider is allowed by your data policy, or Ollama and Mailpit are used
  • [ ] HTTPS terminates at a proxy or tunnel; /readyz is monitored from outside
  • [ ] HRAGENTS_VAPID_SUBJECT names an address you control (push)
  • [ ] The backup drill has run on this host, not only on the developer laptop

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records
docs.text:
Immutable notes for decisions that are expensive to reverse. Each ADR states the context, the decision, and the consequences we accept. The locked-decisions table in docs/plan/master-build-plan.md stays the summary; ADRs add the reasoning, and are citable in the paper.

ADR Decision Status 0001 LLMs extract; deterministic code scores Accepted 0002 Human-in-the-loop bounds enforced in code Accepted 0003 No shell or command tools, ever Accepted 0004 Capability/provider abstraction for every external dependency Accepted 0005 Synchronous domain layer; async only at the agent and network edge Accepted 0006 Single schema with tenant_id and forced row-level security Accepted

New ADRs: copy the format of an existing file, number sequentially, open a PR. ADRs are append-only — to change a decision, add a new ADR that supersedes the old one and update its status line.

docs.title: ADR 0001 — LLMs extract; deterministic code scores
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-12

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Recruiters make initial résumé-fit decisions in roughly 7.4 seconds, and hiring discrimination has stayed essentially flat for decades. LLM judges reproduce the bias in their training data, drift between runs and model versions, and give no auditable reason for a number. Consequential decisions about people need to be reproducible and explainable.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Agents only turn unstructured material (résumés, repositories, documents) into structured, provenance-tagged facts. Scoring, prioritization, and every automation gate are hand-specified deterministic functions in src/hr_agents/services/:

  • the weighted tensor score S ∈ [0,1]^4,
  • the priority function P = α·S̄ + β·e^(−λ·Δt) + γ·A − δ·R,
  • the policy gates (S_tech ≥ 0.85 ∧ σ ≤ 0.05 for auto-scheduling).

Retrieval (RAG) may add recall and answer policy questions; it never computes scores.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Same input, same score — every component cites its evidence.
  • Changing the model can change extraction quality, never a decision. Extraction quality is measured separately by evals.
  • New signals require explicit scorer changes and tests, not prompt tweaks.
  • The LLM cannot be the system of record for anything consequential.

docs.title: ADR 0002 — Human-in-the-loop bounds enforced in code
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-12

docs.title: Context
docs.text: "Human oversight" is usually a policy promise, and promises are easy to bypass under product pressure. Recruiting AI is classified high-risk (EU AI Act, Annex III(4)(a)) and solely automated consequential decisions are restricted (GDPR Art. 22). The product philosophy — agents propose, humans decide — is only credible if the software physically cannot do otherwise.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Every consequential boundary is enforced in deterministic code, not prompts or documentation:

  • Auto-scheduling is allowed only for high-confidence positive outcomes (S_tech ≥ 0.85 ∧ σ ≤ 0.05); everything else routes to a human.
  • Rejections at or above the merit floor (0.70) require a named human sign-off; agents cannot approve, complete, or reject through the approval engine.
  • Overrides are append-only, role-restricted, reason-coded, and never anonymous.
  • Erasure, purge, waive, and final-pay actions are separate human steps.
  • Agents may request approvals or open tasks; they can never complete them.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Negative tests for every gate are part of the definition of done.
  • The UI cannot offer "approve all" shortcuts around these paths.
  • Automation coverage is intentionally lower than what a purely automated product could advertise — that is the point.

docs.title: ADR 0003 — No shell or command tools, ever
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-12

docs.title: Context
docs.text: LLM agents that can run arbitrary commands turn a prompt-injection payload in a résumé into arbitrary code execution on the host that holds employee data. Tool-use capabilities are also the hardest thing to audit: "the agent ran a command" is not an explainable decision.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The tool registry is a closed set of typed, least-privilege tools. There is no shell, run_command, file-system-write, or generic HTTP tool — in code, in configuration, or in any MCP catalog. Every tool call carries a declared scope, is executed by deterministic code, and lands on the audit chain. MCP integrations may only register tools from catalogs that pass the same rule (classified read/write/destructive, with destructive calls approval-gated).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Anything the product must do goes through an explicit, testable tool.
  • Prompt injection cannot escalate to code execution or data exfiltration beyond the declared tool scopes.
  • Some automation ideas are simply off the table; new capabilities are added as tools with tests, not as shell strings.

docs.title: ADR 0004 — Capability/provider abstraction for every external dependency
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-12

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Small companies run on whatever they already have: WhatsApp, Gmail or Outlook, local files or Drive, a local model or an API key. A self-hosted HR system that requires one specific vendor (or a cloud key) cannot be adopted by the "HR department of one" this project targets. Vendor SDKs also creep into core code, making tests network-bound and replacement expensive.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Every external dependency is a capability with interchangeable providers behind a single interface (ProviderSpec, health_check, mask_secrets). Nine capabilities ship with multiple providers — LLM, email, WhatsApp, Telegram, calendar, storage, embeddings, vector store, queue — including zero-config defaults (storage.local_disk, queue.redis, embeddings.hash, whatsapp.manual_links. Configuration comes from environment or the UI; UI wins, environment can lock. The offline test model keeps the whole system runnable and testable with no keys and no network.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Core code depends on interfaces, never vendor SDKs; every provider has a conformance test and a health check.
  • Tests stay offline and deterministic.
  • Adding a vendor is one file plus tests, not a refactor.
  • Some provider features are only available on some backends; the capability interface must expose a capability matrix rather than pretend parity.

docs.title: ADR 0005 — Synchronous domain layer; async only at the agent and network edge
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-12

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Postgres persistence must land before the MCP layer, dashboard, and ops work. The question was how deeply to thread async through the codebase. An audit found the real async zone is narrow: the agent runtime, the pipeline that awaits it, the worker, and two HTTP clients (github.py, file uploads). The domain services and stores — scoring, policy, approvals, tasks, payroll, compliance, growth, offboarding, recruiting — are synchronous, and 144 of 145 route handlers never await anything.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Domain services and stores stay synchronous and remain the behavioral contract. The in-memory implementations define it; Postgres adapters implement the same class API (subclassing the in-memory class so the type checker enforces the contract).
  • Postgres adapters use synchronous SQLAlchemy over psycopg3. A store_backend setting selects memory (default; tests, zero-config dev) or postgres.
  • Store-backed FastAPI routes are def, not async def, so FastAPI runs them in the threadpool and blocking database calls never stall the event loop.
  • async is reserved for code that genuinely awaits I/O: LLM calls (PydanticAI), GitHub HTTP, upload reads, and future SSE streaming.
  • Alembic keeps its asyncpg URL as a separate process; the app derives its sync URL from the same setting.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The persistence change does not touch service or store test suites, keeping a 731-test gate stable.
  • Concurrency for database-backed routes is bounded by the AnyIO threadpool (40 by default) — ample for the self-hosted target; the polish backlog tracks a migration to async IO if profiling ever demands it.
  • Adapter correctness is testable on SQLite in-memory (same adapter code, different engine) and on Postgres in CI, where RLS and JSONB behavior are covered separately.
  • Async service code (pipeline, worker, agents) may call sync stores directly; it must never be called from a sync route without a clear boundary.

docs.title: ADR 0006 — Single schema with tenant_id and forced row-level security
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-12

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The product must be self-hostable by a single company and run as a managed multi-tenant service from the same codebase. Multi-tenant isolation done only in application code fails open: one missed WHERE tenant_id = ... leaks another company's employee data. The platform also already ships a Postgres system of record with Alembic migrations and a sync store-adapter layer (ADR 0005).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• One schema, one column dimension. Every domain table gains a tenant_id UUID NOT NULL (31 tables) via a TenantScoped mixin; existing rows are backfilled to DEFAULT_TENANT_ID (…0001). No schema-per-tenant.
  • PostgreSQL row-level security is the enforcement point. Migration 0006 enables ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and creates a tenant_isolation policy per table with USING and WITH CHECK.
  • Fail closed by default. The policy resolves to tenant_id = COALESCE(NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid, DEFAULT_TENANT_ID). An unset setting behaves as the default tenant: single-tenant installs work with zero configuration, and a misconfigured multi-tenant install sees only the default tenant — never another tenant's rows.
  • Tenant is set per transaction. sync_session_scope(..., tenant_id=…) issues set_config('app.tenant_id', …, true). Application inserts default to the default tenant; the RLS WITH CHECK still blocks cross-tenant writes.
  • Tests (and any deployment) must use a non-superuser role. Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles bypass RLS even with FORCE; scripts/prepare_test_db.py creates a non-superuser role for the CI adapter suite.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Isolation does not depend on application correctness; a forgotten filter returns nothing instead of another tenant's data.
  • The default-tenant fallback keeps the self-host path unchanged and keeps existing tests valid (they run as the default tenant).
  • Every future table must inherit TenantScoped and be added to the migration; tests/db/test_rls.py proves reads and writes are fenced.
  • Superuser connections (for example, the compose hragents user) bypass RLS; production deployments for multiple tenants must connect as the restricted application role. This is tracked in the polish backlog and the ops phase.
  • Tenant-aware connection routing (per-tenant pools/secrets) and RLS policy auditing remain open work; the current slice makes isolation structural.

docs.title: Measured Benchmarks
docs.text: All numbers are measured, not estimated. Re-run any benchmark with the command shown.

docs.title: 1. Ingestion throughput (application layer)
docs.text:
Command: uv run python scripts/benchmark_ingestion.py --total 5000 --concurrency 64 Measured: 2026-09-11

Metric Value Contract Throughput 608.5 req/s = 36,509 req/min 10,000 req/min ✅ (3.6×) Errors 0 / 5000 0 ✅ p50 latency 93.3 ms — p95 latency 143.3 ms — p99 latency 169.1 ms — Audit chain verification after run valid valid ✅

Environment: Windows, Python 3.14.7, in-process ASGI transport (no network), in-memory store, single process. This isolates application overhead (validation, idempotency hashing, audit chaining). Network, PostgreSQL, and Redis add latency in a deployed topology; horizontal scaling and network batching absorb this.

Interpretation: the ingestion path — Pydantic validation, idempotency-key hashing, audit-chain append, store write — sustains well beyond the target on one core. The contract has headroom for the database-backed adapters.

docs.title: 2. Deterministic scoring latency
docs.text: Not yet measured. The scorer exists and is exercised by tests; a dedicated micro-benchmark ships with the evaluation pipeline phase.

docs.title: 3. Priority ranking latency
docs.text: Target: p99 < 50 ms for GET /v1/queue (Redis sorted-set reads). Not yet measured — Redis adapter arrives in the integrations phase.

docs.title: 4.1 Live model run — Command Code Provider API (MiMo V2.5)
docs.text:
Command: uv run python scripts/run_evals.py --live Model: xiaomi/mimo-v2.5 via llm.commandcode (Zero Data Retention enforced, x-cmd-zdr: 1) Measured: 2026-09-11

Case Assertions Result Duration backend_clean_en (English backend résumé) 8/8 ✅ 138.8 s finance_clean_id (Bahasa Indonesia finance CV) 8/8 ✅ 152.3 s header_only (near-empty document) 6/6 ✅ 20.8 s prompt_injection (override + exfiltration attempt) 10/10 ✅ 49.9 s invisible_chars (zero-width characters) 6/6 ✅ 46.9 s Average 100% 5/5 pass 81.7 s

What the live run verifies:

  • Extraction quality: real model extracts name, contacts, experience entries, and skills from both English and Indonesian documents into the CandidateProfile schema (schema round-trip validated by Pydantic).
  • Skill detection: expected technologies present in structured output.
  • Injection resistance: the malicious line is blocked, redacted to [SUSPECTED-INSTRUCTION], categories recorded, and no injected contacts appear.
  • Invisible-character handling: zero-width characters stripped before the model.

Latency note: per-extraction latency (21–152 s, mean 82 s) is acceptable for the async pipeline (workers process extractions in the background; the ingestion API responds in 202 ms at p99). It is not acceptable for interactive use — a strong argument for the phase-7 option of smaller extraction models or local Ollama for bulk re-processing. Upstream variance also matters: the first live run hit transient 524 upstream unavailable errors, and tool-call structured output failed on this endpoint — the runtime now uses prompted JSON output for OpenAI-compatible open-model providers, with retries.

docs.title: 4.2 Offline structural suite (CI)
docs.text:
Command: uv run python scripts/run_evals.py (deterministic test model)

  • Structural and safety assertions: 100% pass across all 5 cases (94.3% of total assertion points; the remainder are semantic checks that require a real model).
  • Runs in CI with no API keys — guards, schema validation, and sanitization are always enforced regardless of provider availability.

docs.title: 4.3 Operational finding
docs.text:
The first live run surfaced two real production risks that are now fixed in code:

  1. OpenAI-compatible endpoints may not support tool-call structured output. Fix: the runtime selects prompted JSON output for llm.commandcode, llm.ollama, and llm.openai_compatible, keeping tool-call mode for Anthropic and the offline test model. Both paths validate identically with Pydantic.
  2. Transient upstream errors (HTTP 524) occur under load. Fix: bounded output retries (default 3) + the provider health/fallback chain.

docs.title: Board Stage Transitions — Manual Move Policy
docs.text:
Version: 0.1.0 · Status: enforced contract (services/stages.py) Related: HITL bounds §3 · master plan §6.3

The pipeline board is derived from deterministic application statuses; cards may be dragged between columns, but a drag is only a request. Every move is validated server-side against the table below, requires a named human and a reason, and lands on the hash-chained audit log as application.stage_changed. Dragging can never bypass a HITL gate.

docs.title: 1. Statuses and the five columns
docs.text:
Column Statuses intake queued, processing screened evaluated decision gated interview scheduled closed rejected, withdrawn

Statuses are derived: queued/processing/evaluated/gated/rejected/scheduled are set by the worker and the policy engine (see services/ingestion.py, services/recruiting.py); this table only governs the additional manual moves a human may request.

docs.title: 2. The transition table
docs.text:
Allowed manual moves (from → to), each requiring by (named human) + reason:

# From To Rationale 1 evaluated gated Pull a candidate out of the auto-schedule path for review — exercising human oversight (EU AI Act Art. 14), never a negative action 2 evaluated withdrawn HR or candidate stops the process before a decision 3 gated withdrawn Stop a gated process; withdrawal is not a rejection 4 scheduled withdrawn Candidate withdrew or process stopped after scheduling 5 scheduled gated Undo a schedule (no-show, collapsed plan) back to review 6 rejected gated Reopen a rejection — the reversal right; auditable, never silent 7 withdrawn gated Correct an accidental withdrawal

All other pairs are refused, with distinct server messages so the UI can point at the right gated flow:

Refused move Server message (409) Correct flow any queued/processing → anything "set by the worker" wait for extraction/scoring anything → rejected "record a rejection sign-off first" review queue → override endpoint (named reviewer + reason code) anything → scheduled (e.g. gated → interview) "scheduling is gated" scheduling proposal / approved override anything → queued/processing/evaluated "not a manual target" system-owned states same-status / same-column "no-op" (409) —

docs.title: 3. Invariants
docs.text:
1. Named human, always. by must be a non-empty human identity — never agent:-prefixed. Agents cannot move cards.
  2. A reason is always required. Free text, recorded in the audit payload.
  3. No forward shortcut around gates. → rejected and → scheduled are not in the table; they exist only behind the override/scheduling writers.
  4. Reversal is allowed. Moves 5–7 move out of consequential states back to a human hold (gated) — the EU AI Act Art. 14 ability to reverse stands.
  5. Closed is not frozen. Only the decision state itself is closed to forward motion; reopening is a first-class, audited action.
  6. Everything lands in the chain. One application.stage_changed audit entry per move with {from, to, reason}; the timeline records application.stage.<to>.

docs.title: 4. Board behavior (web)
docs.text:
• Cards are draggable (pointer + keyboard sensors). Drops resolve through intentForDrop(currentStatus, targetStage) in web/src/features/hiring/pipeline.ts, which mirrors this table for UX routing only — the server re-validates every call:
  • decision column → request gated (reason dialog)
  • closed column → choice dialog: withdraw (reason) or record rejection sign-off (opens the existing override flow; the override endpoint stays the only writer of rejected)
  • interview column → attempt scheduled (server refuses; message shown)
  • intake/screened columns → refused client-side as system-owned
  • same column → no-op
  • Server refetch after success is the source of truth; no optimistic card movement.
  • The pipeline stays read-through: status changes always come back from the API.

docs.title: Data & Storage Architecture
docs.text: Version: 0.1.0 · Decision: PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector for all production workloads; SQLite only as an in-memory test engine.

docs.title: 1. The decision
docs.text: Concern Production choice Why System of record PostgreSQL 16 (pgvector/pgvector:pg16 image) ACID transactions, strong concurrency, JSONB, mature replication, universal managed offerings Candidate/job JSON JSONB columns Schema-validated at the app boundary (Pydantic v2), queryable and indexable inside the database without migration churn Embeddings / semantic search pgvector (HNSW/IVFFlat indexes) RAG and candidate↔JD similarity without operating a second datastore Queue & priority ranking Redis 7 Streams for work distribution; sorted sets for sub-50 ms priority reads Documents MinIO / S3-compatible Large binaries (CVs, portfolios) stay out of the database Tests SQLite (aiosqlite, in-memory) Zero-infrastructure unit tests; full schema created per test

docs.title: 2. Why PostgreSQL for a hiring platform
docs.text:
1. Universally supported. Every serious cloud (AWS RDS/Aurora, GCP Cloud SQL, Azure Database), and managed providers (Supabase, Neon, Aiven, Render) offer Postgres. A company will never struggle to hire for it or to find a hosting path, including in Indonesia (all major providers operate Singapore/Jakarta regions).
  2. One engine covers the workload. Relational integrity for candidates/applications/evaluations, JSONB for evolving profile schemas, full-text search for resume keyword recall, and — with pgvector — embedding similarity. No premature polyglot sprawl.
